A sound has a clear pitch when its [partials](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#partial), the pure tones it is made of, sit at or very near whole-number multiples of one frequency. A plucked string's partials do, so it gives a note you could hum; a struck drum's don't, so it gives a thud.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="duo">
    <div>
      <div class="controls"><button class="primary" data-hook="string">▶ Pluck a string</button></div>
      <svg class="spec" id="rulerString" viewBox="0 0 320 96" aria-label="The frequencies in a plucked string's sound, as multiples of the lowest: they sit on the whole-number lines"></svg>
    </div>
    <div>
      <div class="controls"><button class="primary" data-hook="drum">▶ Strike a drum</button></div>
      <svg class="spec" id="rulerDrum" viewBox="0 0 320 96" aria-label="The frequencies in a struck drum's sound, as multiples of the lowest: they fall between the whole-number lines"></svg>
    </div>
  </div>
  <p class="cap">Call this the <em>pitch ruler</em>. Its gray lines mark whole-number multiples, 1×, 2×, 3×, …, of one base frequency, here the lowest in each sound. Each blue stem is one frequency in the sound; taller means it starts stronger, for an idealized pluck and strike. Both objects are idealized: a perfectly flexible string at 196 Hz, plucked a fifth of the way along (so 5× is missing), and an ideal round drumhead whose lowest frequency is 140 Hz, struck about a third of the way out from its center. Their frequencies are computed for these ideal objects (post 2 works out the string, post 3 the drum); the fading times are modelling choices.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

The reason, in one sentence: **partials on the multiples of one frequency add up to a sound that repeats at that rate, and the ear hears the repetition rate as the pitch, even when no partial sits there.** In the demo, the string's stems sit on the lines, at exactly 1, 2, 3, … times the lowest; the drum's sit at 1, 1.59, 2.14, 2.30, … times the lowest, and no frequency in the range we hear as pitch fits them all closely. This post explains why that decides between a note and a thud, using no differential equations.

## Four aspects of a sound {#four-aspects}

We hear four things in a sound: pitch, loudness, timbre and duration. All four are facts about hearing, measured by asking listeners, not mathematics.[^aspects]

**Sound** is the air pressure $p(t)$ at a listener, as a function of time. The simplest sound is a *pure tone*, the sound of a tuning fork: a pressure swing $a\cos(2\pi f t + \varphi)$ about the average air pressure, with frequency $f$ in [hertz](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#hertz) (cycles per second), size $a$, and phase $\varphi$, which says where in its cycle it starts.

A **partial** is one pure-tone component of a sound, with its own frequency, size and fading. An instrument left to ring after a pluck or a strike sounds, to a good approximation, a sum of partials:
$$
p(t) = \sum_k a_k\, e^{-t/\tau_k} \cos(2\pi f_k t + \varphi_k),
$$
with frequencies $f_k$, starting sizes $a_k$, phases $\varphi_k$ and fading times $\tau_k$: every $\tau_k$ seconds, partial $k$ shrinks by a factor of $e \approx 2.7$. Each partial comes from one of the instrument's [modes](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#mode), a shape the object swings in at one frequency, such as a string swinging as one arc, or as two halves in opposite directions; the body and the room pass them on, adding some ringing of their own. [Post 2](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd) derives this form for a string, and the appendix [*When does an equation have a spectrum?*](../when-an-equation-has-a-spectrum/index.qmd) in general; what it leaves out, such as breath, is noise.

A **harmonic** is a partial at a whole-number multiple $n f$ of a base frequency $f$, the $n$-th harmonic; a *harmonic sound* is one whose partials are all harmonics of one base. An [overtone](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#partial) is any partial above the lowest, so for a harmonic sound the first overtone is the second harmonic.

### Pitch

**Pitch** is how high or low a sound is heard, measured as the frequency of the pure tone that listeners match it to.[^pitchdef] Pitch that can carry a melody is heard for repetition rates (defined [below](#why-whole-numbers-repeat)) from about 30 Hz,[^pressnitzer] and for pure tones up to about 4 or 5 kHz, the traditional upper limit.[^oxenham] Call this *the range we hear as pitch*.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls"><button class="primary" data-s="pure220">▶ Pure tone, 220 Hz</button><button class="primary" data-s="rich220">▶ Partials at 220, 440, 660, … Hz</button><button data-s="pure440">▶ Pure tone, 440 Hz</button></div>
  <p class="cap">The second sound has ten partials, at 1, 2, …, 10 times 220 Hz, with sizes 1, 1/2, …, 1/10. It sounds richer than the first and just as high, so its pitch is 220 Hz. The third is an octave higher.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

### Loudness

**Loudness** is how strong a sound seems. It is set mainly by the sound pressure level: 10 dB more is ten times the power and sounds about twice as loud.[^stevens1] It also depends on frequency: at the same level, a low tone sounds quieter than a mid-range one.[^iso1]

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>Decibels, equal-loudness contours and the power law</summary>

The *sound pressure level* is $20\log_{10}(p_{\mathrm{rms}}/20\,\mu\mathrm{Pa})$ decibels (dB), with $p_{\mathrm{rms}}$ the root-mean-square pressure, the square root of the average squared pressure swing; the *intensity*, the power carried through each square metre, grows as $p_{\mathrm{rms}}^2$, so 10 dB more is ten times the intensity. By the *equal-loudness contours* of ISO 226, which give the level at which pure tones of each frequency sound equally loud to young listeners, a 100 Hz tone needs about 79 dB to match a 1 kHz tone at 60 dB (ISO 226:2023, [*Acoustics — Normal equal-loudness-level contours*](https://www.iso.org/standard/83117.html); the level is computed from the formula of the 2003 edition, from which the 2023 values differ by at most 0.6 dB, as the standard's foreword states). At equal intensity, partials spread beyond a certain width in frequency sound louder than partials bunched together (E. Zwicker, G. Flottorp and S. S. Stevens, ["Critical band width in loudness summation"](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1908963), *J. Acoust. Soc. Am.* 29 (1957), 548–557). Loudness grows roughly as the 0.3 power of intensity, so 10 dB more sounds about twice as loud, since $10^{0.3} \approx 2$ (S. S. Stevens, ["On the psychophysical law"](https://doi.org/10.1037/h0046162), *Psychological Review* 64 (1957), 153–181; Wikipedia, [Stevens's power law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stevens%27s_power_law)).

</details>
:::

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls"><span style="font-family:var(--f-ui);font-size:0.9rem;color:var(--muted)">Same size of pressure swing:</span><button class="primary" data-s="l100">▶ 100 Hz</button><button class="primary" data-s="l1000">▶ 1000 Hz</button><button class="primary" data-s="l3000">▶ 3000 Hz</button><button data-s="lAll">▶ All three in turn</button></div>
  <div class="controls"><span style="font-family:var(--f-ui);font-size:0.9rem;color:var(--muted)">1000 Hz, three levels:</span><button class="primary" data-s="lSteps">▶ 0, then −10, then −20 dB</button></div>
  <p class="cap">First row: three pure tones with exactly the same size of pressure swing in the signal. With good headphones the 100 Hz tone sounds much quieter than the other two; that is the ear's equal-loudness contour. Small laptop and phone speakers play 100 Hz weakly, which exaggerates the effect, and the level at your ear depends on your volume setting, so the numbers in the text apply only roughly. Second row: one tone, stepped down by 10 dB twice; each step sounds about half as loud.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

### Timbre

**Timbre** is what tells apart two sounds of the same loudness and pitch.[^timbredef] It is mostly the partials' sizes and how they change, the start especially.[^timbre] It also includes how far the partials sit from whole-number multiples, how the sound starts and fades ([attack and decay](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#attack-decay)), noise and transients that are not modes (bow noise, breath, hammer thump), and fixed resonances that stay put whatever note is played ([formants](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#formant): a violin's body, a clarinet's tone-hole cutoff).[^formants]

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>The evidence, and the formants</summary>

Removing the onsets of recorded instrument tones cut listeners' accuracy at naming the instruments by about 15 percentage points (E. Saldanha and J. F. Corso, ["Timbre cues and the identification of musical instruments"](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.1919317), *J. Acoust. Soc. Am.* 36 (1964), 2021–2026, as summarized in K. Siedenburg, [Specifying the perceptual relevance of onset transients for musical instrument identification](https://www.uni-oldenburg.de/f/6/dept/mediphysik/ag/musik-wahrnehmung/siedenburg2019transients.pdf), *J. Acoust. Soc. Am.* 145 (2019), 1078–1087). Listeners also hear a finger hitting a piano key and the key hitting bottom (W. Goebl, R. Bresin and I. Fujinaga, [Perception of touch quality in piano tones](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.4896461), *J. Acoust. Soc. Am.* 136 (2014), 2839–2850). A violin's body favors certain bands of frequency whatever the note, as a voice's formants do (M. Schleske, [Introduction to violin acoustics: sound](https://schleske.de/en/research/introduction-violin-acoustics/introduction/sound.html)). Above a cutoff frequency, roughly 1 to 1.5 kHz on a clarinet, sound waves travel on past the open tone holes instead of being turned back by them, and that cutoff depends little on the fingering (E. Moers and J. Kergomard, "On the cutoff frequency of clarinet-like instruments. Geometrical versus acoustical regularity", *Acta Acustica united with Acustica* 97 (2011), 984–996, [arXiv:1101.4742](https://ar5iv.labs.arxiv.org/html/1101.4742); J. Wolfe and colleagues, [Clarinet acoustics: F3](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/music/clarinet/F3.html), UNSW, on waves passing an open tone hole more easily at higher frequencies).

</details>
:::

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls"><button class="primary" data-s="tPure">▶ Pure tone</button><button class="primary" data-s="tBright">▶ Every harmonic</button><button class="primary" data-s="tHollow">▶ Odd harmonics only</button><button class="primary" data-s="tPluck">▶ Every harmonic, plucked</button></div>
  <p class="cap">Four sounds with the same pitch, 220 Hz. The first three are steady and have the same power, which makes them roughly, not exactly, equally loud: one partial; twelve harmonics with sizes 1, 1/2, 1/3, …; and the odd ones of those, which sounds hollow, like a clarinet. The fourth has the second's partials but starts suddenly and fades, the higher partials faster, like a pluck.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

### Duration

**Duration** is how long a note sounds. A ringing instrument's note lasts as long as its fading times allow, unless the player damps it: a key released, a mute, or a hand on the head; a bass drummer stops a note with a leg or a towel on the head.[^aleo] A bowed or blown note lasts as long as the player keeps going. How a note fades is part of its timbre; how long it lasts is its duration.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls"><span style="font-family:var(--f-ui);font-size:0.9rem;color:var(--muted)">Plucked:</span><button class="primary" data-s="dRing">▶ Let it ring</button><button class="primary" data-s="dDamp">▶ Damp it after 0.35 s</button></div>
  <div class="controls"><span style="font-family:var(--f-ui);font-size:0.9rem;color:var(--muted)">Bowed:</span><button class="primary" data-s="dBow05">▶ Half a second</button><button class="primary" data-s="dBow2">▶ Two seconds</button></div>
  <p class="cap">A string at 196 Hz. Plucked, it fades on its own unless damped; the damped note has the same partials, all made to die within about a tenth of a second. Bowed, it is a steady tone (partials 1, 1/2, 1/3, … of a repeating motion) that lasts as long as the bow moves.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

For an instrument left to ring, all four are heard from three things about its partials: where they sit, how strong they are and how fast they fade. Pitch is heard mainly from where they sit; loudness from their strengths, weighted by frequency; timbre from all three, especially early on, plus sounds such as breath or bow noise; duration from the fading and from when the player stops or damps the note. Bowed and blown notes are different ([route 4 below](#four-routes)). The rest of this post asks where the partials must sit for a clear pitch.

## Why whole numbers repeat {#why-whole-numbers-repeat}

Two pure tones repeat together only when their frequency ratio is a fraction. Take 220 Hz and 330 Hz, in the ratio 3 : 2: after two cycles of the lower tone the upper one has completed three, so the sum begins again, 110 times a second. In general, for a ratio $j/k$ in lowest terms, the sum repeats every $k$ cycles of the lower tone, at the rate $f_1/k$. At 1.59 : 1, which is 159/100, that takes 100 cycles: 2.2 times a second for a lower tone at 220 Hz, far below the pitch range.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls"><button id="r2" class="primary">▶ 2 : 1</button><button id="r15" class="primary">▶ 3 : 2</button><button id="r159" class="primary">▶ 1.59 : 1 (a drum)</button><button id="rPlay">Play the slider's ratio</button></div>
  <div class="slider"><label for="ratio">Ratio</label><input type="range" id="ratio" min="1" max="3" step="0.01" value="2"><output id="ratioOut">2.00×</output></div>
  <div class="readout" id="ratioMsg"></div>
  <canvas id="ratioWave" style="height:120px" aria-label="Sum of two tones over six cycles of the lower one"></canvas>
  <p class="cap">Two pure tones, the lower at 220 Hz. Gray ticks mark cycles of the lower tone. At 2 : 1 the sum repeats every cycle; at 3 : 2 every two; at 1.59 : 1 it lines up only after 100 cycles, far off the right of this picture.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

The same holds for any number of steady partials: their sum repeats exactly when all their frequencies are whole-number multiples of one frequency, and then it repeats at the largest such frequency. A signal $p$ is [periodic](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#periodic) with period $P > 0$ if $p(t+P) = p(t)$ for every $t$, and the **repetition rate** of a sound whose partials are steady and exact whole-number multiples of a common frequency is 1 over its shortest period, which is that largest common frequency. That the sum repeats *only* for fractions needs one more fact, that sinusoids of different frequencies cannot cancel one another.

::: {.result}
**Precisely.** Let
$$
p(t) = a_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{n} a_k\cos(2\pi f_k t + \varphi_k),
$$
with distinct frequencies $f_k > 0$ and sizes $a_k \ne 0$. A time $P > 0$ is a period of $p$ exactly when every $f_k$ is a whole-number multiple of $1/P$. So $p$ is periodic exactly when every ratio $f_k/f_1$ is a fraction, and then its shortest period is $1/g$, where $g$ is the largest frequency of which every $f_k$ is a whole-number multiple.
:::

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Proof</span>Sinusoids of different frequencies are independent, so a period must fit every partial <span class="needs">integrals of products of cosines, and divisibility</span></summary>

*Lemma.* Let $0 < g_1 < \dots < g_m$, and suppose that $c + \sum_{j=1}^m \big(\alpha_j\cos(2\pi g_j t) + \beta_j\sin(2\pi g_j t)\big) = 0$ for every $t$. Then $c = 0$ and every $\alpha_j$ and $\beta_j$ is $0$.

*Proof of the lemma.* For a function $h$, write $\langle h\rangle = \lim_{T\to\infty} \frac{1}{2T}\int_{-T}^{T} h(t)\,dt$ for its long-run average, when the limit exists. For $\gamma \ne 0$, $\int_{-T}^{T}\cos(2\pi\gamma t)\,dt = \sin(2\pi\gamma T)/(\pi\gamma)$ stays bounded as $T$ grows, so $\langle\cos(2\pi\gamma t)\rangle = 0$; and $\langle 1\rangle = 1$. The product formulas $2\cos x\cos y = \cos(x-y) + \cos(x+y)$ and $2\sin x\sin y = \cos(x-y) - \cos(x+y)$ then give, for $a, b > 0$, $\langle\cos(2\pi a t)\cos(2\pi b t)\rangle = \langle\sin(2\pi a t)\sin(2\pi b t)\rangle = \tfrac12$ if $a = b$ and $0$ if $a \ne b$. A product of a sine and a cosine is an odd function, so its integral over $[-T, T]$ is $0$, and so is its average. Multiply the assumed identity by $\cos(2\pi g_j t)$ and average: every term vanishes except $\alpha_j/2$, by the averages just computed, so $\alpha_j = 0$. Multiplying by $\sin(2\pi g_j t)$ gives $\beta_j = 0$ in the same way. What remains is $c = 0$.

*Proof of the statement.* If every $f_kP$ is a whole number, each cosine completes whole cycles in time $P$, so $p(t + P) = p(t)$. Conversely, suppose $p(t+P) = p(t)$ for every $t$, and write $\theta_k = 2\pi f_k t + \varphi_k$ and $\delta_k = 2\pi f_k P$. By the identity $\cos(\theta + \delta) - \cos\theta = -2\sin(\delta/2)\sin(\theta + \delta/2)$,
$$
0 = p(t+P) - p(t) = \sum_{k=1}^n -2a_k\sin(\pi f_kP)\,\sin\!\big(2\pi f_k t + \varphi_k + \pi f_kP\big).
$$
Expanding each term into $\alpha_k\cos(2\pi f_k t) + \beta_k\sin(2\pi f_k t)$ gives $\alpha_k^2 + \beta_k^2 = 4a_k^2\sin^2(\pi f_kP)$. The lemma, with $c = 0$, makes every $\alpha_k$ and $\beta_k$ zero, so $a_k\sin(\pi f_kP) = 0$; since $a_k \ne 0$ by hypothesis, $\sin(\pi f_k P) = 0$, which means $f_kP$ is a whole number. This proves the first sentence.

*The shortest period.* If $p$ has a period $P$, the first sentence makes every $f_kP$ a whole number, so $f_k/f_1 = (f_kP)/(f_1P)$ is a fraction. Conversely, suppose every $f_k/f_1$ is a fraction. Over a common denominator $N$, $f_k = n_k h$ with $h = f_1/N$ and whole numbers $n_k$. Let $d$ be the greatest common divisor of $n_1, \dots, n_n$ and $g = dh$; then $f_k = m_kg$ with whole numbers $m_k = n_k/d$ whose greatest common divisor is $1$. By the first sentence, $P$ is a period exactly when every $m_k\,gP$ is a whole number. If $gP$ is a whole number, so is every $m_k\,gP$. Conversely, Bézout's identity (whole numbers whose greatest common divisor is $1$ have a combination with whole-number coefficients equal to $1$) gives whole numbers $u_k$ with $\sum_k u_km_k = 1$, so $gP = \sum_k u_k\,(m_k\,gP)$ is a whole number. So the periods are exactly the whole-number multiples of $1/g$, and the shortest is $1/g$. Finally, if every $f_k$ is a whole-number multiple of some $g'$, then $1/g'$ is a period, hence a multiple of $1/g$, so $g' \le g$: $g$ is the largest such frequency.

*Check on the examples.* Partials at 440, 660 and 880 Hz have $h = 220$, $n_k = 2, 3, 4$, $d = 1$, so $g = 220$ Hz although no partial sits there. Tones at 100 and 159 Hz have $g = 1$ Hz: the sum repeats once a second.

</details>
:::

For real instruments, whose partials fade or sit only near the multiples, the repetition rate is the largest frequency in the range we hear as pitch that the partials fit within a stated tolerance. A sound that fades cannot repeat exactly, but it can nearly: if every partial sits on a multiple of $g$ and fades with the same time $\tau$, each period is the one before shrunk by the factor $e^{-1/(g\tau)}$, by 0.45% at $g = 220$ Hz and $\tau = 1$ s. How near the multiples is near enough is a fact about hearing: a low partial mistuned by more than about 1 to 3%, depending on the listener, stands out as a separate tone.[^mgp1] Within 2%, the middle of that range, the lowest strong partials of the drum in the first demo fit no frequency above about 20 Hz, below the pitch range; the string's fit 196 Hz exactly.

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Precisely</span>How the drum fails to fit, at different tolerances</summary>

Take the partials of the drum in the first demo up to 3.2 times the lowest that start with at least a tenth of the strongest one's size: 1, 1.593, 2.295, 2.653 and 3.155 times 140 Hz. (Its partials at 2.136 and 2.917 start with only about 2% of the strongest's size, because the strike point or the listening point sits near a still line of their modes.) Call a frequency $g$ a fit within a tolerance $\epsilon$ if each partial lies within the fraction $\epsilon$ of a whole-number multiple $ng$ with $n \ge 1$. A computer search over $g$ gives the largest fit; adding the drum's higher partials could only lower it.

| Tolerance | Largest fit $g$ |
|:--|:--|
| 1% | about 14 Hz |
| 2% | about 20 Hz |
| 3% | about 46 Hz |

*Why a fading sound cannot repeat exactly.* If $p(t+P) = p(t)$ for every $t$, then $p(t) = p(t + mP)$ for every whole number $m$, and for a sound that dies away this tends to $0$ as $m$ grows, so $p$ is zero. A piano's partials, slightly sharp of the lines, also nearly repeat.

Within 3%, a base of about 46 Hz fits as its 3rd, 5th, 7th, 8th and 10th multiples, each off by up to 3%, with nothing at the base or at its 2nd or 4th multiple. The 3% figure is generous. It comes from a different measurement by the same authors: in an earlier study, a single mistuned low partial of an otherwise exact harmonic sound kept counting fully toward its pitch up to about 3% (B. C. J. Moore, B. R. Glasberg and R. W. Peters, ["Relative dominance of individual partials in determining the pitch of complex tones"](https://doi.org/10.1121/1.391936), *J. Acoust. Soc. Am.* 77 (1985), 1853–1860, as summarized in C. J. Darwin, A. Buffa and R. L. H. M. Smits, [Pitch of simultaneous complex sounds with a single mistuned component](https://www.ioa.org.uk/system/files/publications/CJ%20DARWIN%20A%20BUFFA%20RLHM%20SMITS%20PITCH%20OF%20SIMULTANEOUS%20COMPLEX%20SOUNDS%20WITH%20A%20SINGLE%20MISTUNED%20COMPONENT.pdf), *Proc. Inst. Acoust.* 12, Part 10 (1990), 499–505), whereas the 1 to 3% above is where a partial starts to be heard out on its own (their 1986 study), and here every partial is off at once. What the ear makes of such a sound is a question about hearing; in the first demo, it is a thud.

</details>
:::

## The missing fundamental {#missing-fundamental}

For a single tone, the ear hears the repetition rate as the pitch, even when no partial sits at it.[^moorepitch] Play the note, then the same note without its 220 Hz partial, and watch the wave.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls">
    <button id="nBright" class="primary">▶ The note</button><button id="nMissing" class="primary">▶ Without its 220 Hz partial</button>
    <button id="nPlay">Play again</button>
  </div>
  <canvas id="nWave" style="height:120px" aria-label="Waveform over three repetitions"></canvas>
  <svg class="spec" id="nSpec" viewBox="0 0 320 90" style="max-width:520px" aria-label="Strength of each partial"></svg>
  <div class="readout" id="nRead"></div>
  <details class="more"><summary>Mix your own</summary>
    <div class="controls" style="margin-top:0.5rem"><button id="nPure">Pure tone</button><button id="nHollow">Hollow, like a clarinet</button></div>
    <div id="nSliders" class="hsliders"></div>
  </details>
  <p class="cap">The wave over three cycles of 220 Hz; gray ticks mark each 1/220 of a second. Stems: how strong each partial is, at 1, 2, 3, … times 220 Hz, on the pitch ruler. The readout gives the repetition rate, the largest frequency of which every partial present is a whole-number multiple.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

The wave changes shape but still repeats every 1/220 of a second, since 440, 660, 880, … Hz are all multiples of 220 Hz, and the pitch stays. Hearing the pitch without its [fundamental](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#fundamental) is the *missing-fundamental* effect; it keeps a deep voice's pitch over a telephone that carries little below about 300 Hz.[^mf] Keep only 2×, 4×, 6× and 8× in "Mix your own", and the pitch jumps an [octave](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#octave).

### Beats {#beats}

Two close partials fit no series in the pitch range, and the ear hears one tone that swells and fades. For two pure tones of equal size, the sum-to-product formula gives
$$
\cos(2\pi f_1 t) + \cos(2\pi f_2 t) = 2\cos\big(\pi (f_2 - f_1) t\big)\,\cos\big(\pi (f_1 + f_2) t\big),
$$
a tone at the average frequency whose size swells and fades $|f_2 - f_1|$ times a second: [beats](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#beats).[^moorebeats] Tones at 220 and 222 Hz repeat together exactly twice a second, far below the pitch range; you hear a 221 Hz tone wobbling twice a second. Faster beats sound rough, and tones far enough apart sound as two smooth tones.[^pl]

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls"><button class="primary" data-beat="2">▶ 220 + 222 Hz</button><button class="primary" data-beat="8">▶ 220 + 228 Hz</button><button class="primary" data-beat="25">▶ 220 + 245 Hz</button><button class="primary" data-beat="110">▶ 220 + 330 Hz</button></div>
  <div class="readout" id="beatRead"></div>
  <canvas id="beatWave" style="height:110px" aria-label="The sum of the two tones over one second"></canvas>
  <p class="cap">The sum of two equal pure tones over one second. Its outline swells and shrinks as many times a second as the two frequencies differ: 2, 8 and 25 times; at 110 Hz apart the swells come too fast to see here, and you hear two smooth tones.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

### Exceptions to the pitch rule {#exceptions}

Three kinds of sound break the rule.

*Chords.* The ear sorts the partials into several series and hears several pitches. C4 and G4 tuned to an exact 3 : 2 have all their partials on multiples of 130.8 Hz (C3), so together they repeat 130.8 times a second; yet you hear two notes, because the ear hears two sets of harmonics with different bases as two sounds.[^bregman]

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls"><button class="primary" data-s="cC4">▶ C4</button><button class="primary" data-s="cG4">▶ G4</button><button class="primary" data-s="cBoth">▶ C4 and G4 together</button><button data-s="cC3">▶ C3, the pair's repetition rate</button></div>
  <p class="cap">Each note has eight harmonics, with sizes 1, 1/2, …, 1/8: C4 at 261.6 Hz, G4 at exactly 3/2 of that, 392.4 Hz. Together they repeat 130.8 times a second, the rate of the last sound, which is not what the pair sounds like.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

*Bells and kettledrums.* A harmonic subset of the partials sets the pitch, and the ear may choose an octave above the base. A bell is heard roughly an octave below its main partial, the nominal, often with no partial at the pitch heard.[^hibbert] A kettledrum is named an octave above the base its main partials fit.[^timp1] The fold gives the partials; [the drums in post 3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#drums) give the kettledrum's modes.

*Strongly stretched partials.* Partials running sharp of the lines, as on a stiff piano string, pull the pitch up;[^jaatinen] beyond the tolerance [above](#why-whole-numbers-repeat), a partial is heard out on its own.[^mgp2]

::: {.derive}
<details><summary><span class="label">Details</span>The bell's and the kettledrum's partials</summary>

*The bell.* In a well-tuned church bell the main partials, the hum, prime, tierce, quint and nominal, sit near 0.5, 1, 1.2, 1.5 and 2 times the prime, and two more, the superquint and the octave nominal, near 3 and 4 times (W. A. Hibbert, [The upper partials of bells](https://www.hibberts.co.uk/the-upper-partials-of-bells/)). The strike note, the pitch the bell is heard at, is close to the prime (Wikipedia, [Strike tone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strike_tone)). The nominal, superquint and octave nominal, nearly in the ratios 2 : 3 : 4, are heard as harmonics of a missing fundamental, the strike note, which lies roughly an octave below the nominal (W. A. Hibbert, [The strike note of bells](https://www.hibberts.co.uk/?p=701), first published in *The Ringing World*, 20 June 2003, p. 586). It can differ from half the nominal by about a quarter of a semitone, and often no partial sits exactly at it, a puzzle Rayleigh noted in 1890; which partials set the note also depends on the bell's size (W. A. Hibbert, [What note do we hear when a bell rings?](https://www.hibberts.co.uk/what-note-do-we-hear-when-a-bell-rings/)). Measured from the hum, the main partials sit at 1, 2, 2.4, 3, 4, 6 and 8: whole numbers, except the tierce, a minor third above the prime. Without the tierce, the main partials fit the hum as base, yet the bell is heard an octave higher.

*The kettledrum.* A kettledrum's air pulls one set of its modes near 2, 3, 4 and 5 times a base, yet players name the note an octave higher, at the lowest of the set, the drum's principal tone. A kettledrum measured by Benade, tuned to C3, had its principal tone at 130.8 Hz and partials at about 1.50, 2.00, 2.49 and 2.98 times it, close to 3, 4, 5 and 6 times half of it, together with others off this pattern (HyperPhysics, [The Timpani](https://hyperphysics.gsu.edu/hbase/Music/timpani.html), tabulating A. H. Benade, [*Fundamentals of Musical Acoustics*](https://archive.org/details/fundamentalsofmu0000bena), Oxford University Press, 1976). On C2, 65.4 Hz, that set forms a near-harmonic series, and HyperPhysics notes that the missing-fundamental effect might then give the pitch C2; the drum is named for its principal tone, C3. Vienna's Institute of Musical Acoustics names the principal tone ("Grundton") as the mode with one still line through the center, and notes that the drum's many partials off whole-number ratios make its exact pitch hard to pin down (Institute of Musical Acoustics (Wiener Klangstil), University of Music and Performing Arts Vienna, [The Viennese timpani](https://www.mdw.ac.at/iwk/wiener-pauke/?l=en)).

</details>
:::

## Four routes to a clear pitch {#four-routes}

Instruments reach a clear pitch by four routes: modes on the whole numbers by nature, modes moved there by design, off-line partials suppressed, or a drive that repeats.

```{=html}
<svg class="fig" viewBox="0 0 320 112" role="img" aria-label="The first three modes of a string: one arc, two halves, three thirds, at 1, 2 and 3 times the lowest frequency"><path class="dash" d="M 40 22 L 280 22"/><path class="acc" d="M 40 22 C 126.4 7.7 193.6 7.7 280.0 22"/><path class="acc" opacity="0.35" d="M 40 22 C 126.4 36.3 193.6 36.3 280.0 22"/><circle cx="40" cy="22" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="280" cy="22" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><text x="290" y="26">1×</text><path class="dash" d="M 40 56 L 280 56"/><path class="acc" d="M 40 56 C 83.2 41.7 116.8 41.7 160.0 56 C 203.2 70.3 236.8 70.3 280.0 56"/><path class="acc" opacity="0.35" d="M 40 56 C 83.2 70.3 116.8 70.3 160.0 56 C 203.2 41.7 236.8 41.7 280.0 56"/><circle cx="40" cy="56" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="280" cy="56" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><text x="290" y="60">2×</text><path class="dash" d="M 40 90 L 280 90"/><path class="acc" d="M 40 90 C 68.8 75.7 91.2 75.7 120.0 90 C 148.8 104.3 171.2 104.3 200.0 90 C 228.8 75.7 251.2 75.7 280.0 90"/><path class="acc" opacity="0.35" d="M 40 90 C 68.8 104.3 91.2 104.3 120.0 90 C 148.8 75.7 171.2 75.7 200.0 90 C 228.8 104.3 251.2 104.3 280.0 90"/><circle cx="40" cy="90" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><circle cx="280" cy="90" r="2.5" class="fillacc"/><text x="290" y="94">3×</text></svg>
```

1. **By nature: strings and air columns.** A string's $n$-th mode fits $n$ half-waves between its ends (the picture), and every wave travels along the string at the same speed, so an ideal [string](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd)'s $n$-th mode swings at exactly $n$ times the lowest frequency. A flute's air column, open at both ends, resonates at every whole-number multiple, and a [clarinet](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#clarinet)'s, closed at the reed, at the odd ones.[^wolfefc] Guitars and harps take this route, and the [piano](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#piano) nearly, since stiffness pushes its partials slightly sharp. Bowed strings and winds start here too; route 4 makes their partials exact.
2. **By design.** A kettledrum's air slows its coarse shapes most, pulling one set of modes near 2 : 3 : 4 : 5 ([the drums in post 3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#drums)). A marimba bar's arch, cut underneath, moves its first overtone from 2.76 times the lowest, for a uniform bar, to 4 times; a xylophone's shallower cut, to 3 times.[^bars] A patch of paste loading the middle of a tabla's head brings its modes near whole-number ratios.[^raman] Founders shape and tune a bell so that most of its principal partials sit on multiples of half the strike note, all but the minor-third tierce.[^bellfound]
3. **By suppression.** Some off-line partials are weak or die fast: a [kalimba](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#kalimba) tine's overtones, at 6.27 and 17.55 times its lowest, die within a fraction of a second,[^chapman] and a struck glockenspiel bar's modes all die out quickly except the lowest.[^scavone] Others are never started: a strike at a still point of a mode does not set that mode going, and timpanists strike between halfway and three-quarters of the way out,[^timp2] near the still lines of several modes that do not fit the note.
4. **By a periodic drive: bow and breath.** A bow or a breath keeps feeding the motion, which settles into a single repeating cycle, so its partials sit at exact whole-number multiples, whatever the object's own modes:[^wolfehh] a bow's stick and slip drive all of a string's resonances at exactly harmonic ratios, and a harmonica reed, whose own overtones are off the lines, chops the air into identical puffs ([the harmonica in post 3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#harmonica)). The [resonator](../instruments-as-operators/glossary.qmd#resonator)'s modes only shape which partials are strong, and the player sets loudness and duration.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls"><span style="font-family:var(--f-ui);font-size:0.9rem;color:var(--muted)">1 · By nature:</span><button class="primary" data-s="rString">▶ Plucked string</button></div>
  <div class="controls"><span style="font-family:var(--f-ui);font-size:0.9rem;color:var(--muted)">2 · By design:</span><button class="primary" data-s="rBar276">▶ Uniform bar</button><button class="primary" data-s="rBar4">▶ Undercut bar</button></div>
  <div class="controls"><span style="font-family:var(--f-ui);font-size:0.9rem;color:var(--muted)">3 · Suppressed:</span><button class="primary" data-s="rKal">▶ Kalimba tine</button><button data-s="rKalLong">▶ The same, overtones ringing as long</button></div>
  <div class="controls"><span style="font-family:var(--f-ui);font-size:0.9rem;color:var(--muted)">4 · Driven:</span><button class="primary" data-s="rReedP">▶ Harmonica reed, plucked</button><button class="primary" data-s="rReedB">▶ The same reed, blown</button></div>
  <p class="cap">Row 2: a bar's lowest two partials at middle C, with the overtone at 2.76 times the lowest (a uniform bar) or at 4 times (an undercut marimba bar); sizes and fading times illustrative. Row 3: a kalimba tine at C5, its overtones at 6.27 and 17.55 times the lowest, fading fast as measured, then the same partials made to ring as long as the lowest. Row 4: the reed has the tine's frequencies when plucked; blown, it sounds a steady tone with partials at whole-number multiples only.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

Why does a vibrating object have modes at all, and why do their frequencies form a list? For the string, [post 2](../one-string-end-to-end/index.qmd) answers this completely; the appendix [*When does an equation have a spectrum?*](../when-an-equation-has-a-spectrum/index.qmd) answers it in general.

## Dynamics change timbre too {#dynamics-and-timbre}

A harder blow sounds louder and brighter. A piano hammer's felt gets harder the more it is squashed, so a fast hammer stays on the string for a shorter time and starts more high partials;[^aj] with a felt that stayed equally soft, a loud note would be a soft note turned up.[^russell] [The piano in post 3](../other-instruments-same-recipe/index.qmd#piano) takes it up.

```{=html}
<div class="ins">
<div class="panel">
  <div class="controls"><button class="primary" data-s="hSoft">▶ Soft blow</button><button class="primary" data-s="hHard">▶ Hard blow</button><button data-s="hSoftUp">▶ Soft blow, turned up</button></div>
  <p class="cap">Middle C on a model piano string. The hard blow has stronger high partials and an average level 10 dB higher; the third button plays the soft blow 10 dB louder, at the hard blow's average level, and it still sounds duller. How fast the partials fall off with number is an illustrative choice, not computed from a model of the felt.</p>
</div>
</div>
```

<script src="core.js"></script>
<script>
(function () {
  "use strict";
  var C = Core, M = C.models;
  // Every sound below is played with gain G. core.js sends it through a gain of 0.55 and a compressor with threshold -10 dB;
  // buffers peak at 0.8 at most, so 0.8 * G * 0.55 = 0.264 stays below the threshold and relative levels are exact.
  var G = 0.6;
  function peakOf(b) { var d = b.getChannelData(0), pk = 0; for (var i = 0; i < d.length; i++) pk = Math.max(pk, Math.abs(d[i])); return pk; }
  function scale(b, s) { var d = b.getChannelData(0); for (var i = 0; i < d.length; i++) d[i] *= s; return b; }
  function toPeak(b, v) { var pk = peakOf(b); return pk > 0 ? scale(b, v / pk) : b; }
  function rmsOf(b, sec) { var d = b.getChannelData(0), n = Math.min(d.length, Math.floor(sec * b.sampleRate)), s = 0; for (var i = 0; i < n; i++) s += d[i] * d[i]; return Math.sqrt(s / n); }
  // synth(segs, dur): segments {t0, t1, parts: [{f, amp, tau}], ramp (s), sharp (2 ms attack), cut: {at, tau}}; tau omitted = steady.
  function synth(segs, dur) {
    var a = C.ac(), SR = a.sampleRate, N = Math.max(1, Math.floor(dur * SR)), b = a.createBuffer(1, N, SR), d = b.getChannelData(0);
    segs.forEach(function (s) {
      var n0 = Math.floor(s.t0 * SR), n1 = Math.min(N, Math.floor(s.t1 * SR)), len = n1 - n0, r = Math.max(1, Math.floor((s.ramp || 0.02) * SR)), ra = s.sharp ? Math.floor(0.002 * SR) : r;
      s.parts.forEach(function (p) {
        if (p.f > SR / 2.3 || !p.amp) return;
        var w = 2 * Math.PI * p.f / SR, dec = p.tau ? Math.exp(-1 / (p.tau * SR)) : 1, e = p.amp;
        for (var n = 0; n < len; n++) { d[n0 + n] += e * Math.sin(w * n); e *= dec; }
      });
      for (var n = 0; n < len; n++) {
        var env = 1;
        if (n < ra) env = 0.5 - 0.5 * Math.cos(Math.PI * n / ra);
        if (len - n < r) env *= 0.5 - 0.5 * Math.cos(Math.PI * (len - n) / r);
        if (s.cut && n / SR > s.cut.at) env *= Math.exp(-(n / SR - s.cut.at) / s.cut.tau);
        d[n0 + n] *= env;
      }
    });
    return b;
  }
  function one(parts, dur, opt) { opt = opt || {}; return synth([{ t0: 0, t1: dur, parts: parts, ramp: opt.ramp, sharp: opt.sharp, cut: opt.cut }], dur); }
  function harm(f, n, amp, odd, tau) { var out = []; for (var k = 1; k <= n; k++) { if (odd && k % 2 === 0) continue; out.push({ f: f * k, amp: amp(k), tau: tau ? tau(k) : 0 }); } return out; }
  function inv(k) { return 1 / k; }
  function play(b, g) { C.play(b, g == null ? G : g); }

  // ---- 1 · the opening pair, on the pitch ruler ----
  var HOOK = {
    string: { parts: function () { return M.violin.partials({ pluck: 0.2 }); }, f: 196, dur: 2.6, svg: "rulerString" },
    drum: { parts: function () { return M.drum.partials({ r: 0.35 }); }, f: 140, dur: 2.4, svg: "rulerDrum" }
  };
  function drawRulers() {
    Object.keys(HOOK).forEach(function (k) { C.stems(document.getElementById(HOOK[k].svg), HOOK[k].parts(), { W: 320, H: 96, rmax: 6, fs: 9, sw: 2.5, noOff: true }); });
  }
  document.querySelectorAll("[data-hook]").forEach(function (b) {
    b.addEventListener("click", function () { var h = HOOK[b.getAttribute("data-hook")]; play(C.render(C.toHz(h.parts(), h.f), h.dur)); });
  });

  // ---- sounds for the four aspects, the exceptions, the routes and the hammer ----
  var C4 = 261.63, timbre = null;
  function timbreSet() {
    if (timbre) return timbre;
    var power = 0.125, d = 1.3; // every steady sound gets sum of amp^2 / 2 = power
    function norm(parts) { var s = 0; parts.forEach(function (p) { s += p.amp * p.amp / 2; }); var k = Math.sqrt(power / s); return parts.map(function (p) { return { f: p.f, amp: p.amp * k, tau: p.tau }; }); }
    var bright = norm(harm(220, 12, inv));
    var set = {
      tPure: one(norm([{ f: 220, amp: 1 }]), d, { ramp: 0.03 }),

    pure440: function () { play(toPeak(one([{ f: 440, amp: 1 }], 1.3, { ramp: 0.03 }), 0.8)); },

    l3000: function () { play(one([{ f: 3000, amp: 0.8 }], 1.2, { ramp: 0.04 })); },

    lSteps: function () { play(synth([0, -10, -20].map(function (db, i) { return { t0: 1.3 * i, t1: 1.3 * i + 1, parts: [{ f: 1000, amp: 0.8 * Math.pow(10, db / 20) }], ramp: 0.04 }; }), 3.8)); },
    tPure: function () { play(timbreSet().tPure); },
    tBright: function () { play(timbreSet().tBright); },
    tHollow: function () { play(timbreSet().tHollow); },
    tPluck: function () { play(timbreSet().tPluck); },
    dRing: function () { play(toPeak(one(pluck196(), 3, { sharp: true, ramp: 0.2 }), 0.8)); },

    dBow05: function () { play(toPeak(one(bowed196(), 0.5, { ramp: 0.05 }), 0.8)); },
    dBow2: function () { play(toPeak(one(bowed196(), 2, { ramp: 0.05 }), 0.8)); },
    cC4: function () { play(toPeak(one(harm(C4, 8, inv), 1.6, { ramp: 0.03 }), 0.8)); },

  // ---- 3 · two tones and their ratio ----
  var rs = document.getElementById("ratio"), ro = document.getElementById("ratioOut"), msg = document.getElementById("ratioMsg"), cv = document.getElementById("ratioWave");
  function period(r) { for (var q = 1; q <= 4; q++) { var p = Math.round(r * q); if (Math.abs(p / q - r) < 0.003) return q; } return 0; }
  function wave() {
    var r = parseFloat(rs.value), q = period(r), d = C.fit(cv), W = cv.width, H = cv.height, ctx = cv.getContext("2d"), T = 6;
    ro.textContent = r.toFixed(2) + "×";
    msg.innerHTML = q ? "repeats every <b>" + q + "</b> cycle" + (q > 1 ? "s" : "") + " of the lower tone: <b>" + (220 / q).toFixed(q === 3 ? 1 : 0) + "</b> times a second" : "does not line up within these six cycles";
    ctx.clearRect(0, 0, W, H); ctx.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--grid"); ctx.lineWidth = d;
    for (var k = 0; k <= T; k++) { var x = k / T * W; ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(x, H - 8 * d); ctx.lineTo(x, H); ctx.stroke(); }
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(0, H / 2); ctx.lineTo(W, H / 2); ctx.stroke();
    ctx.strokeStyle = C.rgb("--accent"); ctx.lineWidth = 2 * d; ctx.beginPath();
    for (var i = 0; i <= W; i++) { var t = i / W * T, y = Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * t) + 0.7 * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * r * t), py = H / 2 - y / 1.75 * (H / 2 - 10 * d); if (i) ctx.lineTo(i, py); else ctx.moveTo(i, py); }

  document.getElementById("r2").addEventListener("click", function () { setR(2); playR(); });
  document.getElementById("r15").addEventListener("click", function () { setR(1.5); playR(); });
  document.getElementById("r159").addEventListener("click", function () { setR(1.59); playR(); });
  document.getElementById("rPlay").addEventListener("click", playR);

  // ---- 4 · the note and its missing fundamental ----
  var F = 220, NH = 8, amp = [1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0];
  var box = document.getElementById("nSliders"), inputs = [];
  for (var n = 1; n <= NH; n++) {

    dv.innerHTML = '<label for="h' + n + '" style="min-width:5.5rem">' + (n + " × 220 Hz") + '</label><input type="range" id="h' + n + '" min="0" max="1" step="0.01"><output id="h' + n + 'o"></output>';
    box.appendChild(dv);

  for (var m = 1; m <= NH; m++) (function (i) {

  document.getElementById("nPure").addEventListener("click", function () { setAll([1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]); });
  document.getElementById("nBright").addEventListener("click", function () { setAll([1, 1 / 2, 1 / 3, 1 / 4, 1 / 5, 1 / 6, 1 / 7, 1 / 8]); playMix(); });
  document.getElementById("nHollow").addEventListener("click", function () { setAll([1, 0, 1 / 3, 0, 1 / 5, 0, 1 / 7, 0]); });
  document.getElementById("nMissing").addEventListener("click", function () { setAll([0, 1 / 2, 1 / 3, 1 / 4, 1 / 5, 1 / 6, 1 / 7, 1 / 8]); playMix(); });
  document.getElementById("nPlay").addEventListener("click", function () { if (amp.some(function (a) { return a > 0; })) playMix(); });

  function draw() {
    inputs.forEach(function (el, i) { document.getElementById("h" + (i + 1) + "o").textContent = amp[i].toFixed(2); });
    var d = C.fit(wv), W = wv.width, H = wv.height, x = wv.getContext("2d"), periods = 3, mx = 0, ys = [];

  }
